items.title: 52060_Eddie Barefield oral history interview
items.q: And I had already told Bill Crump, the first man, that I couldn't read but he didn't believe it.

ctx.x: So one day we were in some little town and the leader called a rehearsal. So we had this rehearsal and I'll never forget the orchestration he put up, it was called "Sam, Sam, the accordion man." And this thing had a six bar -- eight bar introduction. And naturally, after the six bar the tenor saxophone break. And in those days when you had a break the band always stopped. Well, when they stopped at the end of the six bars, I stopped, too.

He said, "You've got a tenor break there." So I said okay, and they started again. And I flew into one of my things. He stopped the band again and he said, "it's written there what you're supposed to play." And there I was, shown up right away. And he said, "you mean to tell me you've been sitting in this band all the time and you couldn't read?" I said, well, yes, sir, that's the way it's been." And I had already told Bill Crump, the first man, that I couldn't read but he didn't believe it. He always said, oh,…

So then right away he said, 'well, I'm going to have to fire you because, I mean, we have to have somebody that can read.' So I started packing my horn up and I started off the bandstand and the people that owned the band were two Jewish people, the Faths, Mr. Howard Fath.
